newsitem.title: JAPAN: Many voters uncommitted in Japan elections--survey.
newsitem.headline: Many voters uncommitted in Japan elections--survey.

text.p: Three weeks before Japan holds general elections, more voters are uncommitted than support the most popular party, a newspaper survey showed on Tuesday.

Thirty-one percent of voters said they favoured no political party in the October 20 elections, against 28 percent expressing support for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).

The Democratic Party, a reformist bloc formed at the weekend in a bid to attract unaffiliated voters, outpolled the larger main opposition party to become Japan's second most popular political party, the daily Asahi Shimbun reported.
The survey, published a week before campaigning begins for the elections, showed the Democrats had a support rate of nine percent.

Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), the main opposition party which is headed by former LDP powerbroker Ichiro Ozawa, garnered only seven percent support in the telephone survey of 2,000 voters, the liberal daily said.

The Social Democratic Party (SDP) and New Party Sakigake, partners in the LDP-led ruling coalition formed in mid-1994, scored five percent and one percent, respectively. The Japan Communist Party got a support rating of three percent.

The Democratic Party, formed mainly by defectors from the Social Democrats and Sakigake, is seen by many analysts as a probable LDP coalition partner if, as projected, the conservative LDP fails to capture a majority in the 500-seat Lower House of parliament.

Voters surveyed by the Asahi said they preferred an LDP-led coalition government over a purely LDP administration by a margin of 41 percent to 11 percent. Sixteen percent said they preferred a coalition government excluding the LDP.
